strengths: Well-motivated problem: Identifies genuine limitations of existing instruction-guided segmentation methods that handle only simple NP prompts; hierarchical instruction formulation (concept/simple/complex) is intuitive and well-justified

Substantial dataset contribution: HMPL-Instruct is comprehensive with 44,109 images, 849,792 instructions, 213,160 part-level masks, systematic coverage of instruction hierarchies and granularities, and human-in-the-loop construction with multiple validation stages

Rigorous experimental validation: Comprehensive ablation studies demonstrating each component's contribution, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, evaluation on both benchmarks and custom dataset, multi-faceted qualitative analysis with clear insights

Technically sound approach: Cascaded adapter design with clear motivation, multiple specialized losses targeting different aspects, well-designed multi-stage training curriculum, results preserve SAM3's concept capability while adding instruction following
Clear presentation and comprehensive appendices: Well-structured paper with informative figures, detailed implementation details, visualization results, and data construction pipeline documentation
weaknesses: Computational complexity inadequately addressed: No runtime or memory footprint comparisons; multi-stage training with cascaded adapters likely expensive; MLLM-based instruction generation/validation pipeline cost is not analyzed; scalability implications of human-in-the-loop validation not discussed

Limited baseline diversity: Primary comparisons only against SAM3 and SAM3 Agent (same family); missing comparisons with other recent instruction-guided segmentation methods; SAM3 Agent baseline unfairly compared as it wasn't designed for this task

Generalization concerns: All experiments on natural images from PACO-LVIS/COCO; no cross-domain evaluation to medical imaging, satellite imagery, or other visual domains; unclear how hierarchical instruction formulation generalizes beyond this domain

Design choices insufficiently justified: Three-level instruction hierarchy not empirically validated as optimal; weighting scheme in contrastive loss (Eq. 3) lacks theoretical justification; parent-rank anchoring assumes instruction hierarchies that may not always hold; loss weight balance appears empirically tuned

Dataset bias and representativeness: MLLM-based generation may introduce systematic biases; human-in-the-loop filtering with 100% accuracy requirement may bias toward unambiguous instances; limited discussion of whether instruction distribution represents real-world usage

Incomplete analysis of limitations: Brief Limitations section lacking failure mode analysis; no evaluation of ambiguous instructions, negations, or complex logical operators; missing robustness analysis to instruction paraphrasing; no human evaluation of instruction-following quality beyond mask metrics

Limited technical novelty: Cascaded adapters are standard transfer learning approach; loss functions are adaptations of existing techniques; primary novelty is problem formulation and dataset rather than novel architectures or algorithms

Evaluation limitations: gIoU and PaSe don't directly measure instruction-following quality; no inter-annotator agreement reported; missing sensitivity analysis for instruction complexity or ambiguity distribution

Methodological concerns: Freezing SAM3 backbone may unnecessarily limit task-specific learning; multi-stage training strategy lacks clear convergence criteria or stage transition ablation; reproducibility difficult due to MLLM randomness in annotation pipeline
Moderate performance improvements: Concept-level improvement (29.5→30.8 gIoU) is incremental; overall improvements consistent but not dramatic, limiting impact claims

strengths: Clear problem formulation: Well-motivated extension of SAM3 to handle complex natural language instructions beyond short noun phrases
Sensible technical approach: Hierarchical instruction taxonomy (concept→simple→complex) with cascaded adapters reflects linguistic complexity progression naturally
Thorough data pipeline: Three-stage annotation-inspection-correction workflow ensures high-quality instruction-mask pairs with diverse semantic types
Comprehensive ablations: Table 2 convincingly demonstrates contribution of curriculum learning, distribution alignment, and hard-region supervision
Parameter efficiency: 1.1B parameters vs 8.8B for agent-based alternatives, with single-pass inference
Clear presentation: Well-written with intuitive figures and logical flow
weaknesses: Explicitly marked as 'preliminary results' with comprehensive evaluation ongoing; unsuitable submission for a fully-realized contribution
Limited evaluation scope: Only evaluated on authors' own PACO-LVIS-Instruct dataset; no validation on established benchmarks (ReferIt, G-Ref, ReasonSeg)
Questionable ACL relevance: Core contribution is image segmentation (computer vision), not NLP; language understanding component is straightforward attribute/spatial reasoning
Incremental technical novelty: Cascaded adapters, curriculum learning, and alignment losses are established techniques; main contribution is combination, not fundamental innovation
Moderate performance gains: 54.0 vs 41.6 on simple (12.4 gIoU improvement) but only 51.0 vs 48.2 on complex (2.8 gIoU); authors explicitly state state-of-the-art is out of scope
Dataset concerns: PACO-LVIS-Instruct constructed using MLLMs (Qwen3-VL) introducing systematic biases; no inter-annotator agreement metrics; acknowledged N-to-1 limitation prevents group reasoning
Limited instruction complexity: Despite 'complex' label, instructions remain relatively simple; no multi-step reasoning or handling of 1-to-N group segmentation
No external validation: No zero-shot generalization studies, cross-dataset evaluation, or comparison with other instruction-following segmentation methods
Incomplete analysis: No systematic error analysis, failure case discussion, or investigation of which linguistic phenomena cause difficulties
Significant computational barriers: Data construction requires 32 H100 GPUs, model training 16 H100s, limiting reproducibility; depends on Qwen3-VL availability
